items.title: Tom Stagg Interview, 1969-10-03
items.q: we heard of Lord Richard Eakins as a record producer. Before then he was just an enthusiast from Birmingham.

ctx.x: Graham Russell and a girl, Ray Whittrick, decided to form a Bunk Johnson Appreciation Society, and they were holding once a month meetings in a pub, the Porcupine, just off Charing Cross Road in London. I joined this with my brother at that time, who was beginning to play a little bit of banjo, and we joined it, and the first meeting we ever went to must have been in late 1958, when Graham Russell came out of the Air Force. The first records we heard were the folkways Music of New Orleans, and it was in 1958 I…

about six or eight of them, they had about five records between them. And they had written and asked me, in fact, if they could have Chic and Handy, but they'd left it so late it was impossible to organise anything with Chic and Handy, but we said the next musician we bring to England, we would offer them. We offered them Lewis Nelson, and they jumped at the idea. So we flew with Nelson to Milan. Now Lewis Nelson was the first New Orleans musician ever to go to Italy. And it has worked out today that he's paved…

And this is really sad for England because to us we've gone down a stage. We got to a very good period where British traditional style bands were playing concerts. And big jobs, the Royal Festival Hall, the Conway Hall, which we've already mentioned. The Royal Festival Hall has symphony concerts and symphony orchestras. And the British traditional bands got to this stage where they were playing this type of job. And we now feel as if we've gone down a stage. That the English bands are now playing these pub jobs…
